title: Intel Xeon 6+ SKU List and Value Analysis: Clearwater Forest Runs Wide
gist: Intel's 18A-based Xeon 6+ Clearwater Forest has four SKUs (144-288 cores, ~$4.6K-$15K) with no feature gating; it is a pipe-cleaner for Intel's fabs ahead of 2027's Diamond Rapids. The 288-core 6990E+ wins on throughput and low-TDP per-core efficiency (~1.15W/core vs 2.34-2.60W for AMD EPYC 9965) but carries a ~63% per-core price premium, while the 144-core 6960E+ leads on clocks, cache and memory bandwidth per core.

insights.claim: Xeon 6+ Clearwater Forest is Intel's first server CPU on the 18A process node and has been shipping for just over a quarter.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Confirms 18A is in volume server production, a key milestone for Intel's foundry credibility.
insights.quote: The first server chips based on Intel’s 18A process node
insights.locator: Intel has been shipping its Xeon

insights.claim: Clearwater Forest functions as a pipe-cleaner for Intel's fabs and Foveros Direct 3D packaging lines, with the real test for 18A(-P) server parts being Diamond Rapids in 2027.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Investors should treat Diamond Rapids in 2027, not Clearwater Forest, as the decisive 18A server proof point.
insights.quote: what will be the real big test for Intel 18A(-P) server parts: 2027’s Diamond Rapids
insights.locator: Intel has been shipping its Xeon

insights.claim: Xeon 6+ supply is only now reaching vendors outside the hyperscalers, who typically get a quarter-plus lead on chip supply.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler priority allocation means broader enterprise/OEM revenue from Xeon 6+ lags initial shipments by a quarter or more.
insights.quote: Xeon 6+ chips are finally becoming available to vendors outside the hyperscalers
insights.locator: As part of this process, Intel

themes.theme: SKU stack simplicity and no feature gating

insights.claim: The Xeon 6+ lineup has only 4 physical SKUs spanning 144 to 288 cores and roughly $5K to $15K list price.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A narrow stack signals a focused high-core-count play rather than broad market segmentation.

insights.claim: Intel is not gating features by SKU on Xeon 6+: every part gets 2-socket support, 12 channels of DDR5/MRDIMM, 96 PCIe lanes and Application Energy Telemetry, a break from Intel's historically heavy use of feature-based differentiation.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Dropping feature segmentation suggests Intel is prioritizing competitiveness in dense x86 over upsell margin tactics.
insights.quote: Intel is not gating any features behind specific SKUs, which has historically been a chip-differentiation technique they have used heavily
insights.locator: The good news is that Intel

themes.theme: Power efficiency and the AMD comparison

insights.claim: The 288-core Xeon 6990E+ in high-TDP mode delivers the highest throughput at a 2.8GHz average all-core turbo but draws 450W.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Top-end density comes with rack power demands that matter for power-constrained data centers.

insights.claim: Speed Select (SST-PP) low-TDP mode on the 6990E+ cuts all-core turbo 14% to 2.4GHz while cutting TDP 27% to 330W, a favorable power/frequency trade.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Operators can trade small performance for large power savings, improving perf/watt in power-limited facilities.
insights.quote: drops all-core turbo speeds by 14% to 2.4GHz, while the TDP drops by 27% (120W) to 330W

insights.claim: In low-TDP mode the 6990E+ and 6980E+ reach about 1.15W and 1.14W per core, versus 2.34-2.60W per core for AMD's 192-core EPYC 9965, though AMD's P-cores run two threads each so per-thread figures are in a similar ballpark.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: On a vCPU basis Intel's E-core parts are roughly competitive with AMD, not dramatically ahead, tempering share-gain expectations.
insights.quote: So if you were counting threads/ vCPUs, Intel’s parts are in a similar ballpark.

insights.claim: The 144-core Xeon 6960E+ guarantees 2.4GHz base and 3.0GHz all-core turbo at 330W, about 25% higher clocks than the 6990E+ at the same power, making it the per-core performance sweet spot.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Workloads that cannot scale to 288 cores get better per-core performance and lower cost from the smallest SKU.
insights.quote: for workloads that need many cores but cannot scale to 288 cores, this is a sweet spot
insights.locator: The advantage of going with smaller

insights.claim: Because Intel uses salvaged base dies, L3 cache does not shrink 1:1 with cores, so L3 per core rises from 2MB on the 6990E+ to 2.5MB on the 6970E+ and 3MB on the 6960E+.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Salvaged-die reuse improves yield economics for Intel while giving lower SKUs a cache advantage.
insights.locator: The smallest SKU is also the

insights.claim: With identical 12-channel DDR5-8000 MRDIMM support, memory bandwidth per core doubles from 2.67GB/s on the 288-core SKU to 5.34GB/s on the 144-core SKU.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Memory-bound workloads may be better served by fewer cores per socket, affecting server config mix.

insights.claim: Xeon 6+ list prices are roughly $4,600 (6960E+), $7,700 (6970E+), $9,900 (6980E+) and just under $15,000 (6990E+), with the flagship carrying about a 63% per-core cost premium over the cheapest part.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Steep top-end pricing indicates Intel extracts premium margins on maximum density; list prices are typically discounted.
insights.quote: that is around a 63% premium on per-core costs

insights.claim: Memory costs often dominate server pricing today, so CPU cost-per-core is only one part of total server economics.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Elevated memory pricing shifts server BOM value toward DRAM vendors and dilutes CPU price differences.
insights.quote: memory costs often dominate server pricing these days

insights.claim: Even with only 4 SKUs, compute, memory and cost each have different optimal points, so the lineup can serve a wide range of customers only if they match SKU to workload.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: SKU selection is workload-specific, implying mixed demand across the stack rather than flagship-only sales.
insights.quote: customers need to do their homework to figure out what they need
